01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
annual report
A document describing an organisation’s work and finances over a year.
grant
Money given to help someone study or complete a project.
approve
To officially agree that something may happen.
storage
A place where records or objects are kept.
caption
Words printed beside a photograph.
correction
A published statement fixing an earlier mistake.

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma opened the trust’s annual report on her laptop. Sarah had sent her a link to the accounts, but Emma was still thinking about the anonymous call.

“Ask who signed the payments,” the man had said.

She found a table of grants paid to students in 2011. It gave totals for the year, but not the names of the students or the people who had approved each payment. She checked another page. There was a note about a student support programme. It did not explain how each student had received the money.

Emma called Sarah.

“These totals don't tell us whether any payment was wrong,” Emma said.

“Can we ask for the detailed records?”

“We can ask. But we shouldn't say the money was stolen just because the report doesn't show every name.”

A reply arrived from Fiona Bell. Fiona confirmed that the foundation had held a board meeting in September 2011. She said there might be paper copies of its minutes in storage, but she had not checked the boxes herself. She also explained that the published accounts showed groups of payments, not every individual transaction.

Fiona offered to ask the records team which boxes were still available. She did not promise that they would find anything.

Emma read the message twice. It was a useful answer, but it did not solve the mystery.

That afternoon, she visited the public library. She wanted to see an old local newspaper that had not been fully copied online. In a report about a fundraising event in 2011, she found a photograph of Claire standing beside several students. Malcolm Vale was at the other end of the group. The caption said the foundation had promised travel grants to help students attend courses outside the village.

Emma photographed the page and recorded its date.

The picture proved that the promise had been made in public. It did not show who had received money.

Sarah rang again. “So what do we have?”

“A promise to students, a yearly total, and a question about the individual payments,” Emma said. “Not an answer.”

Before she left, the librarian brought her a second newspaper from the same month. Emma was about to close it when she noticed a small correction printed near the bottom of the page. It referred to the foundation’s student travel scheme.

The correction said that the number of students named in an earlier article had been wrong.

Emma copied the notice. She would need to find the earlier article before she could understand the difference.

For the first time that day, the next step was clear. She needed to compare what the foundation had promised with what its records could actually confirm.
